concept.name: Charm
concept.definition: Charm is the second-order cross sensitivity of an option's value to the underlying price and time: the rate of change of delta with the passage of time, equivalently the rate of change of theta with the underlying price. It measures how a position's directional exposure drifts as expiration approaches.
concept.intuition: Charm is why your hedge moves on its own overnight: as time passes, deltas of OTM options bleed toward zero and ITM deltas toward one, even with the stock unchanged.
concept.mechanics: Charm = -d(delta)/d(tau) = d(theta)/dS = -d2V/(d(tau) dS), typically quoted as delta change per day. It matters most for delta-hedged books held over weekends or into expiration, and aggregate dealer charm is tracked as a driver of hedging flows into the close of large expirations.
concept.failure_modes: Charm accelerates near expiration, so full-day delta-decay estimates become inaccurate exactly when hedges matter most; books hedged Friday can be materially off-hedge Monday purely from charm. As a model quantity it inherits all Black-Scholes input sensitivities.
concept.misconceptions: Charm is not time decay of the option price — that is theta; charm is the time decay of delta. Confusing the two leads hedgers to mis-position for expiration-week drift.
concept.example: An OTM call with delta 0.30 and charm -0.02 per day drifts toward delta 0.24 over a quiet weekend with the stock flat, forcing a hedger to buy back 6 deltas per contract to stay neutral.
